packages.label: מִלּוּי בֶּטֶן וְהַבְּחִירָה הָעַצְמִית
packages.reason: The Torah's central structural category: two seemingly opposite orientations — seeking reward in this world and seeking reward in the next world — are revealed to share the same essential nature: self-oriented appetite. Both are called 'filling the belly' (מִלּוּי בֶּטֶן). The concept of 'portion in life' (חֶלְקָם בַּחַיִּים) and 'Your hidden store' (צְפוּנְךָ, i.e., world to come) are both declared to be aspects of belly-filling. This package represents any service of God that is motivated by personal gain rather than fulfilling God's will.

merge_notes.reason: The Torah explicitly states that both 'חֶלְקָם בַּחַיִּים' (this-world seekers) and 'צְפוּנְךָ' (next-world seekers) are two faces of the same reality — מִלּוּי בֶּטֶן. They are not cause-and-effect but two manifestations of the same self-oriented nature, and therefore belong in the same package.

packages.label: מוֹתָרוֹת וְטִנּוּף
packages.reason: Money accumulated through worldly desire is called מוֹתָרוֹת (surplus/excess) — what is left over after all appetites are satisfied. Children born outside of holiness are also called מוֹתָרוֹת, because they come from the overflow of the brain (שכבת זרע) that exits as a rotten drop (טִפָּה סְרוּחָה). The word עוֹלְלִים (infants/children) is exegetically linked to טִינוּף (filth) via Rashi on Psalm 8. Money and unholy children share the same essential nature: both are the surplus remainder of appetite-driven existence.

merge_notes.reason: The text explicitly states that unholy children are מוֹתָרוֹת in the literal sense — they arise from the brain-overflow (סִרְחוֹן וַעֲכִירַת הַמֹּחַ) as a rotten drop (טִפָּה סְרוּחָה), making טִפָּה סְרוּחָה and מוֹתָרוֹת two expressions of the same surplus/waste reality.
The text cites Rashi: 'עוֹלֵל פֵּרֵשׁ רַשִׁ"י: טִינוּף וְלִכְלוּךְ' — the word עוֹלְלִים is defined as an aspect (בְּחִינַת) of filth, making these two the same essential concept.

packages.label: צֶלֶם דְּמוּת תַּבְנִיתוֹ
packages.reason: Holy children (בָּנִים דִּקְדֻשָּׁה) are explicitly described as a bechina of 'צֶלֶם דְּמוּת תַּבְנִיתוֹ' — God's image and form. When a child is born in holiness, a divine image enters the world. This is the positive mirror of Package 2: where unholy children are surplus and filth, holy children are the completion and manifestation of God's image. The term 'תְּמוּנָתֶךָ' (Your image/form) appearing in the verse is identified as the holy dimension of children.

packages.label: חֲזוֹת פְּנֵי ה' וְהַכָּרָה
packages.label_en: Beholding God's Face and Divine Knowledge
packages.reason: This package represents the highest goal of human service — not reward in this world or the next, but to know and recognize the Creator. David's declaration 'אֲנִי בְּצֶדֶק אֶחֱזֶה פָנֶיךָ' frames the entire Torah. The concepts of 'seeing God's face' (חֲזוֹת פְּנֵי ה') and 'knowing/recognizing God' (הַכָּרַת הַבּוֹרֵא / דַּעַת ה') share the same essential nature — they are different expressions of the direct apprehension of God. Righteousness/justice (צֶדֶק) is described as the path-quality through which one attains this vision, making it part of the same domain.

packages.label: מִמְתִים מֵחֶלֶד — מוֹת טִבְעִי
packages.label_en: Natural Death and Children of This World
packages.reason: The text distinguishes two modes of death: 'מִמְתִים יָדְךָ ה'' (those whose death is decreed by God before their time, as punishment) and 'מִמְתִים מֵחֶלֶד' (those who live out their natural lifespan by natural moisture/vitality until it expires). The latter are declared to be 'בְּנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה' — children of this world who have no share in the world to come. 'לַחוּת שָׁרְשִׁיִּית' (root/natural moisture) is the physiological bechina of natural lifespan. These concepts share the nature of the purely natural-temporal existence that runs its course and ends.
